notes.3:24: "Lord GOD" translates the compound divine title Adonai YHWH, where the Tetragrammaton is pointed with the vowels of Elohim.
notes.4:13: Hebrew reads literally 'the ten words,' the traditional designation for the Ten Commandments.
notes.4:23: The Hebrew verb meaning 'commanded you' here carries the contextual sense 'forbidden you,' referring back to the prohibition against making graven images.
notes.4:37: Hebrew uses singular collective pronouns ('his descendants after him'), referring to the patriarchs as a whole.
notes.4:48: Mount Sion (Hebrew Si'on) is an alternate name for Mount Hermon and is distinct from Mount Zion (Tsiyyon) in Jerusalem.
notes.5:10: The Qere reads "My commandments," which is followed in the translation; the Ketiv reads "His commandments."
notes.5:17: Following the Saints Hebrew Critical Text, the prohibition against adultery stands in verse 17 and murder in verse 18, matching the order attested in the Nash Papyrus and the Septuagint rather than the standard Masoretic sequence.
notes.5:22: The Hebrew phrase translated "and He added no more" indicates that the LORD spoke no further words directly to the whole assembly from the mountain beyond the Ten Commandments.
notes.6:4: The compact Hebrew declaration of the Shema may also be rendered "the LORD our God, the LORD is one" or "the LORD our God is one LORD."
notes.6:7: The Hebrew verb rendered "teach them diligently" comes from a root meaning to sharpen, conveying repeated and incisive instruction.
notes.6:8: The Hebrew term "frontlets" refers to memorial bands or phylacteries bound upon the forehead as a visible sign of devotion to the LORD.
notes.7:2: The Hebrew infinitive absolute construction from the root charam expresses total devotion under the ban, irrevocably setting the Canaanite nations apart for destruction.
notes.7:9: The Masoretic text writes 'His commandments' in a defective spelling without the plural yod, read as the plural 'His commandments' here and again in 8:2.
notes.7:13: The Hebrew terms shegar alafeka and ashterot tsoneka refer respectively to the calving increase of cattle and the lambing offspring of flocks, underscoring covenant fertility.
notes.7:26: The noun cherem ('a thing devoted to destruction') echoes the command of verse 2, warning that bringing forbidden idolatrous objects into a home brings the ban upon the household itself.
notes.8:3: Literally 'everything that goes forth from the mouth of the LORD,' denoting every sustaining decree and provision ordained by God rather than bread alone.
notes.8:9: The Hebrew noun miskenut ('scarcity' or 'poverty') appears only here in the Hebrew Bible, and nechoshet refers to copper ore mined from the hills.
notes.8:15: The Hebrew phrase nachash saraf ('fiery serpent') refers to venomous desert snakes whose bite produces a burning pain, recalling Numbers 21:6.
notes.8:18: Verses 17 and 18 deliberately repeat the Hebrew idiom for acquiring wealth by strength, contrasting human pride with the LORD's covenant empowerment.
notes.9:21: Hebrew literally calls the golden calf "your sin which you had made," naming the idol metonymically after the transgression it embodied.
notes.9:26: The Hebrew divine title here is Adonai YHWH, rendered "Lord GOD" in vocative address to distinguish it from the standalone Tetragrammaton ("the LORD").
notes.9:28: "The land" is paired with a plural verb in Hebrew, referring by metonymy to the inhabitants of Egypt.
notes.10:4: Hebrew literally reads "the ten words," the classic biblical designation for the Ten Commandments.
notes.10:6: Verses 6-7 form a brief third-person historical notice within Moses' speech, recording Aaron's death and Eleazar's succession; Beeroth-bene-jaakan means "wells of the sons of Jaakan."
notes.10:16: "Circumcise the foreskin of your heart" is a covenantal metaphor calling for inward consecration and the removal of spiritual stubbornness.
notes.10:17: "Shows no partiality" translates the Hebrew idiom "does not lift up faces," denoting absolute judicial fairness.
notes.11:2: The Hebrew clause contains an ellipsis ("for not with your children"), supplying the implied verb of speaking as Moses addresses the eyewitness generation rather than their children, resuming the thought in verse 7.
notes.11:13: In verses 13 through 15, Moses' discourse shifts directly into the first-person voice of the LORD ("My commandments... I will give"), emphasizing that the covenant blessings proceed directly from God Himself.
notes.11:24: "Western Sea" translates the Hebrew "hinder sea" (the Mediterranean), reflecting ancient Hebrew directional orientation facing east toward the rising sun.
notes.12:3: "Asherah poles" renders the Hebrew asherim, sacred wooden poles or stylized trees erected at Canaanite shrines in honor of the goddess Asherah.
notes.12:5: The recurring formula "the place which the LORD your God shall choose to put His name there" establishes centralized sanctuary worship in contrast to the scattered high places of Canaan.
notes.12:23: "Life" translates the Hebrew nefesh ("soul" or "life-breath"), grounding the prohibition of consuming blood in the principle that the blood embodies the creature's life.
notes.13:1: In the Masoretic Hebrew versification followed here, this verse opens chapter 13; many English Bibles place it as 12:32, shifting the subsequent verses of chapter 13 by one.
notes.13:14: Hebrew literally reads men, sons of worthlessness (or sons of Belial), an idiom for lawless, corrupt, and destructive persons.
notes.13:16: The Hebrew root behind devoting to destruction (and things devoted to destruction in verse 18) denotes persons or property irrevocably placed under the ban and given over wholly to the LORD for total destruction.
notes.13:17: The Hebrew term rendered wholly is also a sacrificial term denoting a whole burnt offering consumed completely by fire.
notes.14:5: The exact modern species identification of several Hebrew wild-animal names in verse 5 and unclean-bird names in verses 12 through 18 remains uncertain.
notes.14:21: Deuteronomy distinguishes the sojourner (a resident alien dwelling within Israelite towns) from the foreigner (a non-resident outsider).
notes.14:28: Unlike the annual festival tithe brought to the central sanctuary, this third-year tithe was stored locally within each town to support the Levites and the vulnerable.
notes.15:1: Hebrew shemittah denotes the sabbatical seventh-year release or remission of debts among fellow Israelites.
notes.15:18: The concise Hebrew idiom indicates that six years of a bondservant's uncompensated labor was worth twice the cost of a hired worker, or twice a standard three-year hiring term.
notes.15:19: Setting apart every firstborn male of herd and flock recalled the LORD's redemption of Israel's firstborn in Egypt, forbidding their use for ordinary farm labor or shearing.
notes.16:7: The Hebrew verb bishalta broadly means to cook or boil, though in the context of the Passover offering it is traditionally understood alongside the roasting instruction of Exodus 12:9.
notes.16:10: The rare Hebrew noun missat occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and denotes a sufficient measure or proportionate tribute given freely in response to the LORD's blessing.
notes.16:20: The emphatic Hebrew repetition tsedeq tsedeq ("Justice, justice") stresses an uncompromising pursuit of pure righteousness and impartial judgment.
notes.16:21: An "Asherah" was a sacred wooden pole or planted tree linked with Canaanite fertility worship, strictly prohibited beside the altar of the LORD.
notes.17:8: The paired Hebrew phrases—between bloodshed and bloodshed, claim and claim, and assault and assault—represent difficult capital, civil, and bodily-injury cases requiring appeal to the central sanctuary.
notes.17:18: The Hebrew phrase mishneh hattorah hazzot ("a copy of this law") was translated in the Septuagint as to deuteronomion touto, from which the book's English title "Deuteronomy" derives.
notes.18:8: The terse Hebrew phrase levad mimkarav al-ha'avot indicates that any income a Levite retains from selling ancestral family property does not reduce his equal share in sanctuary provisions.
notes.18:10: Making a son or daughter pass through the fire refers to pagan child sacrifice, listed together with divination, sorcery, and necromancy as forbidden practices of the surrounding nations.
notes.18:15: Moses promises that the LORD will raise up a prophet like himself from among Israel to mediate God's word, a promise fulfilled both in Israel's true prophets and ultimately in the Messiah.
notes.19:4: The Hebrew idiom literally reading from yesterday and the third day denotes time past or previously.
notes.19:5: The Hebrew literally reads from the wood, referring to the wooden handle of the ax.
notes.19:14: Landmarks were boundary stones set by earlier generations to demarcate family inheritances.
notes.20:6: The Hebrew verb literally means to make common, referring to enjoying a vineyard's fruit for ordinary use after the initial consecrated years.
notes.20:17: The Hebrew infinitive absolute construction expresses complete devotion to destruction under the sacred ban.
notes.20:19: The rhetorical Hebrew clause contrasts fruit-bearing trees with human combatants, forbidding the wanton destruction of food-producing orchards during a siege.
notes.21:4: The Hebrew expression denotes a ravine with a perennial flowing stream that remains unplowed and unsown.
notes.21:7: The Masoretic Qere reads the plural verb agreeing with our hands, whereas the Ketiv preserves a singular feminine verb form.
notes.21:23: The Hebrew phrase literally reads a curse of God is one who is hanged, referring to the public post-execution display of a corpse under divine judgment.
notes.22:5: The Hebrew phrase rendered 'a man's apparel' literally means 'gear' or 'an article of a man,' encompassing male garments as well as items associated with men such as weapons or equipment.
notes.22:9: The verb translated 'become forfeited' literally means 'become holy' or 'consecrated,' signifying that the mixed yield is withdrawn from ordinary human use and forfeited to the sanctuary.
notes.22:15: Throughout verses 15 through 29, except in verse 19, the Hebrew employs the archaic Pentateuchal spelling of 'young woman' lacking the final feminine letter, while vocalizing it as feminine.
notes.22:19: Hebrew literally reads 'one hundred of silver' here and 'fifty of silver' in verse 29, with the standard weight of a shekel implied.
notes.23:1: Hebrew 23:1 corresponds to 22:30 in most English versions, shifting the verse numbering of chapter 23 by one. To 'uncover his father's skirt' is an idiom for violating his father's marital rights.
notes.23:3: The Hebrew term 'mamzer' denotes the child of a strictly forbidden or incestuous union.
notes.23:5: 'Mesopotamia' translates the Hebrew 'Aram-naharaim,' literally 'Aram of the Two Rivers,' referring to the upper Euphrates region.
notes.23:19: 'The price of a dog' is a biblical idiom for the earnings of a male cult prostitute, echoing the prohibition in verse 18.
notes.23:25: In the Saints Hebrew Critical Text, the provision regarding a neighbor's standing grain stands in verse 25 and that regarding a neighbor's vineyard in verse 26, reversing the order in standard printed Masoretic editions.
notes.24:1: "Some unseemly thing" renders the Hebrew phrase literally meaning "nakedness of a matter," indicating a serious impropriety distinct from adultery, which carried a separate penalty in 22:22.
notes.24:6: Hebrew literally reads "a pair of millstones or an upper millstone"; seizing either part disabled a household's daily grinding of grain, thereby taking a family's livelihood or "life."
notes.24:15: "Sets his heart upon it" translates the Hebrew idiom "lifts up his soul toward it," expressing the poor laborer's urgent dependence on the day's wages.
notes.25:2: "Deserves to be beaten" renders the Hebrew idiom literally meaning "a son of striking."
notes.25:13: "Differing weights" literally reads "a stone and a stone" in Hebrew, referring to stone weights used in balance scales; similarly, verse 14 literally reads "an ephah and an ephah" for dry grain measures.
notes.25:18: "Attacked your rear" translates a Hebrew verb literally meaning "cut off the tail," describing an ambush on the weary stragglers trailing behind Israel's march.
notes.26:5: "A wandering Aramean" may also be translated "a perishing Aramean," referring to the patriarch Jacob during his precarious years in Aram and his later descent into Egypt.
notes.26:14: "In my mourning" refers to bereavement over the dead, which rendered a person ritually unfit to eat consecrated portions; "for the dead" alludes to ancient Near Eastern funerary food offerings.
notes.26:17: The rare Hebrew causative verb used here and reciprocally in verse 18 signifies a solemn, binding covenant declaration between Israel and the LORD.
notes.27:6: "Whole stones" translates Hebrew shlemot, denoting complete, unhewn natural stones untouched by iron tools (compare verse 5).
notes.27:9: "Keep silence" renders a rare Hebrew imperative occurring only here in the Hebrew Bible, calling Israel to hushed, attentive reverence.
notes.27:20: "The covering of his father" literally reads "the skirt" or "edge of his father," a Hebrew idiom for the garment or blanket symbolizing marital union.
notes.27:26: The Masoretic Hebrew reads "the words of this law" without "all," whereas some ancient versions and Galatians 3:10 include "all."
notes.28:22: The Masoretic Text vocalizes this word as "sword"; the same consonants with different vowel points mean "drought," which some interpreters associate with the surrounding terms for heat and crop blight.
notes.28:27: Translates the Masoretic Qere ("tumors" or "hemorrhoids"); the Ketiv reads "swellings."
notes.28:30: Translates the Masoretic Qere ("shall lie with her"), a euphemistic reading for the Ketiv ("shall violate her").
notes.28:32: Literally "and there is not to the power of your hand," a Hebrew idiom expressing complete helplessness.
notes.28:54: "His eye shall be evil" is a Hebrew idiom meaning to look begrudgingly or stingily upon someone, refusing to share.
notes.28:67: Literally "Who will give evening?" and "Who will give morning?", a Hebrew idiom expressing desperate longing.
notes.28:69: Follows the Masoretic Text versification; most English Bibles number this verse as Deuteronomy 29:1.
notes.29:1: In the Masoretic Text, Deuteronomy 29:1-28 corresponds to 29:2-29 in most English Bibles because the covenant superscription appears as 28:69.
notes.29:4: In verses 4-5 Moses shifts directly into first-person divine speech, proclaiming the LORD's wilderness provision as His covenant mediator.
notes.29:9: Literally "your heads, your tribes"; the Masoretic Text juxtaposes the two nouns in apposition to address both the tribal leaders and the tribes as a whole.
notes.29:18: The Hebrew idiom "to sweep away the watered along with the dry" conveys sweeping, indiscriminate ruin, sparing neither the sated nor the craving.
notes.29:28: The Masoretic Text marks the Hebrew words for "for us and for our children forever" with extraordinary dots (puncta extraordinaria), traditionally highlighting Israel's enduring responsibility to obey the revealed law.
notes.30:3: "Restore your fortunes" renders the Hebrew idiom shuv shevut, literally "turn back your captivity," signifying full restoration from exile and affliction.
notes.30:6: "Circumcise your heart" recalls Deuteronomy 10:16, depicting inward spiritual renewal in which the LORD removes stubbornness and enables wholehearted love.
notes.30:11: "Too difficult" translates the Niphal of pala, referring to something too wondrous, cryptic, or beyond human reach and understanding.
notes.31:7: The Masoretic Text reads the Qal verb tavo ("you shall go with this people"), emphasizing Joshua's solidarity with Israel, whereas verse 23 uses the Hiphil tavi ("you shall bring the children of Israel"), emphasizing his leadership.
notes.31:10: The "year of release" (Hebrew shemittah) refers to the seventh-year sabbatical remission of debts prescribed in Deuteronomy 15:1-2, at which time the entire law was to be read publicly during the Feast of Tabernacles.
notes.31:17: Because Hebrew treats "this people" as a collective noun, verses 16-21 alternate between singular and plural pronouns; the quoted lament literally uses the corporate singular ("upon me because my God is not in my midst").
notes.31:21: The Hebrew noun yetser ("inclination") denotes the inward framing, intent, or disposition of the heart, as in Genesis 6:5 and 8:21.
notes.32:5: The Masoretic wording is compact and poignant, literally indicating that Israel's moral blemish disqualifies them from being counted as His true children, in sharp contrast to the Rock's perfection in verse 4.
notes.32:13: The Hebrew text has a minor orthographic ketiv/qere variant for "the heights," with the ketiv written plene and the qere vocalized defectively; both carry the same sense.
notes.32:42: The Hebrew term rendered "long-haired" can refer to warriors with unbound hair vowed for battle, or alternatively to the enemy's "leaders" or "princes."
notes.32:44: The Masoretic Text preserves "Hoshea," Joshua's original name prior to its change by Moses in Numbers 13:16.
notes.33:2: The Ketiv (written text) reads a single word, eshdat, while the Qere (traditional read text, translated here) divides it into two words, esh dat, meaning "a fiery law."
notes.33:5: "Jeshurun" is a poetic and affectionate title for Israel meaning "the upright one."
notes.33:23: "The west" translates the Hebrew yam (literally "sea"), which may refer either to the western region or specifically to the Sea of Chinnereth (Galilee).
notes.33:25: The Hebrew term rendered "bolts" can also be understood as "sandals," and the rare word translated "strength" occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible.
notes.34:2: "The Western Sea" literally translates "the hinder sea," denoting the Mediterranean Sea.
notes.34:5: Lit. at the mouth of the LORD
notes.34:6: The Hebrew verb "buried" leaves its singular subject implicit, traditionally understood as the LORD Himself.
